H&P – Super Detailed

Consult Summary:
34-year-old man with 3-day history of acute watery diarrhea (4–5 times/day) associated with mild abdominal pain, single episode of vomiting, and reduced appetite; no red-flag features identified; managed conservatively with dietary advice and oral rehydration.

History:
• Onset: Diarrhea began 3 days ago.  
• Course: Persisting; neither clearly worsening nor improving.  
• Frequency/Character: 4–5 bowel motions per day; described as watery/loose, variable consistency.  
• Associated symptoms: Mild abdominal pain, one episode of vomiting, mild subjective fever, decreased appetite.  
• Negative review: No blood in stool, no mucus, no severe abdominal pain, no recent travel, no suspicious food intake, no dehydration symptoms reported, still able to maintain oral intake.  
• Self-care to date: No medications taken for diarrhea or abdominal pain.

Past Medical History:
• Asthma – longstanding; patient uses an inhaler named “Lexapro” (exact formulation/dose/route/frequency not documented; clarification required).

Social History:
• No information provided on smoking, alcohol, recreational drugs, occupation, or living circumstances.  
• Reports drinking fluids adequately; comment “mostly it’s been dry and red” unclear.

Family History:
• Father: Hypertension; died of bowel cancer at age 62.  
• No other familial illnesses discussed.

Physical Examination:
• Tele-consultation; no vitals or physical findings documented. Patient subjectively appears well hydrated.

Investigations:
• None performed or ordered at this visit.

Assessment & Plan:
Issue 1: Acute infectious-type diarrhea (likely viral gastroenteritis)
  • Advice:
    – Maintain hydration; drink plenty of water.  
    – Start oral rehydration salts (e.g., Dioralyte) as needed.  
    – Follow a “soft” diet: crackers, toast, jam, mashed/boiled vegetables; avoid dairy (except yogurt/probiotics), meat, fish, and eggs until 48 h symptom-free, then re-introduce gradually.  
  • Red-flag instructions:
    – Seek medical review if stools increase to ≥6–8/day, if blood or mucus appears, if symptoms persist beyond 7 days, or if signs of dehydration develop.  
    – Stool sample and possible antibiotics if blood present or diarrhea prolonged.  
  • Follow-up: Contact service again or attend hospital if above red flags occur.

Issue 2: Asthma (background)
  • Continue current inhaler (“Lexapro”) – dosage/route/frequency to be clarified at future review.  
  • No acute concerns today.

General plan items:
  • Provide written summary in patient’s app for reference.  
  • Encourage patient to clarify inhaler type/name at next review for accurate medication list.

Quality checks:

• Missing/expected elements:  
  – Detailed medication reconciliation (names/doses/routes/frequencies) beyond inhaler.  
  – Detailed allergy review (patient states “none,” but specifics not explored).  
  – Social history (smoking, alcohol, occupation) absent.  
  – Vitals and physical exam not available in tele-visit.

• Internal conflicts: None noted.

• Transcript quality: Generally clear; occasional minor audio gaps/mispronunciations (“Lexapro” inhaler uncertain).
